lead: A missile cannot steer by looking at a target; it needs a number. The guidance law is the rule that turns what the seeker or radar knows about the target into one acceleration command, written a_c or n_c, and the autopilot and fins then make the airframe produce it. Every guidance law in use sits in one of four families: command, homing, navigation and modern. Knowing the family tells you where the computer sits, what it measures, and what can go wrong. Air-to-air, anti-tank and surface-to-air missiles all run on these laws.
prereq: You need: the autopilot idea from Unit 1, Flight Control Systems, since that is the block which receives the guidance command.

blocks.text: Guidance is a loop, not a one-shot sum. Five blocks sit in it, and the last one feeds the first.

items: Seeker or radar measures the target: range R in metres, closing speed, and the angle of the line of sight (LOS), the straight line from missile to target.
The guidance law turns those measurements into one number, the commanded lateral acceleration a_c, in m/s² or in g, where 1 g = 9.81 m/s².
The autopilot compares a_c with the acceleration the airframe is actually pulling and issues fin deflection commands (see 6.7).
Fin servos move the surfaces, the airframe makes lift, and the missile turns.
The seeker measures again. The loop repeats many times a second.

blocks.text: This is feedback control at the outer level. Its bandwidth is low, a few hertz, because the missile body turns far slower than a fin servo. A command that changes faster than the airframe can follow is wasted, and it can excite the body. Guidance laws are therefore designed together with the autopilot, not separately.

Two consequences matter. A command can never be better than the measurement behind it: a noisy LOS rate gives a noisy a_c. And whichever family of law is used, the output is always the same kind of signal, an acceleration command, so the autopilot does not care which law produced it.

Two different questions split the laws. Command and homing answer: where does the guidance computer sit? Navigation and modern answer: what rule does it run? The four names are the labels in everyday use, even though they mix the two questions.

items: Command guidance: the computer stays on the ground, on the launcher or in the launching aircraft, and the missile carries a receiver and an autopilot. In MCLOS (manual command to line of sight) an operator watches missile and target and steers with a joystick. In SACLOS (semi-automatic) the operator only holds a crosshair on the target and the computer works out the command. In beam riding the missile flies inside a radar or laser beam aimed at the target and corrects itself whenever it drifts off the beam centre. Details in 6.3.

Homing guidance: the computer travels inside the missile and the seeker looks at the target itself. Active homing means the missile carries both transmitter and receiver, so it is fire-and-forget. Semi-active means another radar, on the ground or in the launching aircraft, illuminates the target and the missile only receives the reflection. Passive means the missile transmits nothing and listens for heat, reflected light or the target's own radar.

Navigation guidance: the rule is a statement about geometry and can run on the ground or on board. Pursuit points the velocity vector at the target. CLOS keeps the missile on the line from launcher to target. Proportional navigation commands acceleration proportional to the rate at which the LOS is rotating, and is the workhorse of homing missiles. The mathematics is in 6.4 and 6.5.

Modern guidance: optimal laws minimise a cost such as miss distance plus control effort. Differential-game laws treat the target as an opponent who is also optimising. Sliding-mode and H-infinity laws hold stability when the model is wrong. Estimation-based laws fuse seeker and inertial data, often with a Kalman filter, before the law runs. Optimal and robust are the two names most syllabi use.

sections.h3: Classical and modern: two cuts of one set

blocks.text: Some syllabi call pursuit, LOS, CLOS and PN the classical guidance laws and put everything else under modern guidance. That is a division by date and by mathematics, not by hardware. A PN law from the 1950s and a sliding-mode law from the 2010s may run inside the same homing missile, one after the other as the missile flies.

Classical laws assume a target that does not dodge and measurements that are clean. Against a turning tank or a jinking aircraft the miss distance grows unless the missile has acceleration margin to spare. Modern laws attack that gap: they model the target's manoeuvre, or minimise a cost, or drive the error to zero in finite time in spite of the model.

For the exam, keep three labels apart: the family (command, homing, navigation, modern), where the computer sits, and the rule it runs. A semi-active homing missile flying proportional navigation carries all three labels at once.

examples.question: An anti-tank missile is 4 km from its target and closing at 800 m/s. The seeker sees the target 200 m to one side of the missile's present velocity vector. Treating the correction as a constant lateral acceleration starting from zero sideways velocity, find the time to go and the average lateral acceleration needed to remove the error.
steps: Time to go: t = R ÷ v = 4000 m ÷ 800 m/s = 5 s.
With zero initial sideways velocity, the sideways displacement is y = ½ a t².
Rearrange for acceleration: a = 2y ÷ t² = (2 × 200 m) ÷ (5 s)² = 400 m ÷ 25 s² = 16 m/s².
Convert to g: 16 m/s² ÷ 9.81 m/s² per g = 1.63 g.
So the guidance law must call for about 1.6 g of lateral acceleration for 5 s. Whichever family produces that command, the autopilot and fins must deliver this number.
examples.answer: Time to go 5 s, average lateral acceleration 16 m/s², which is about 1.63 g.
examples.check:
v = 800.0
R = 4000.0
y = 200.0
t = R / v
a = 2 * y / t**2
g = a / 9.81
print(t)
print(a)
print(round(g, 2))

traps: Mixing the two divisions. Command and homing say where the computer sits; pursuit, CLOS and PN say what rule it runs. A homing missile can and usually does run PN.
Calling semi-active homing 'command guidance' because the launcher radar does the illuminating. Illuminating is not commanding: the missile still computes its own steering, on board.
Unit slips with g. Writing 16 g instead of 16 m/s², or 1.63 m/s² instead of 1.63 g. Divide or multiply by 9.81 and state which unit you mean.
Assuming modern always beats classical. A well-tuned PN law with enough acceleration margin often beats an optimal law built on a wrong target model.
Thinking CLOS is homing. In CLOS the computer tracks both missile and target from the launch site, so the hardware is command guidance even though the rule is geometric.

quiz.q: Define a guidance law in one sentence.
quiz.a: A rule that converts measurements of the target, such as range, closing speed and line-of-sight angle or rate, into a commanded lateral acceleration for the autopilot.

quiz.q: What is the line of sight, and why does its rate matter?
quiz.a: The straight line joining the missile (or launcher) to the target. Its rotation rate is the main input to proportional navigation, because a non-rotating line of sight means a collision course.

quiz.q: State the one difference that separates command guidance from homing guidance.
quiz.a: Where the guidance computer sits. In command guidance it is outside the missile, on the ground, launcher or aircraft; in homing guidance it is inside the missile. The sensor and the data link follow from that choice.

quiz.q: Why is semi-active homing still homing?
quiz.a: The missile carries the receiver, the seeker and the guidance computer, and it steers itself. The external radar only illuminates the target; it does not compute or send steering commands.

quiz.q: A missile is 3 km from the target, closing at 600 m/s, with a 150 m sideways error. Find the time to go and the constant lateral acceleration needed.
A missile uses command guidance with a CLOS rule. Classify it on both axes and name one weakness the classification reveals.
quiz.a: Command family, because the computer is on the ground; navigation rule CLOS. The weakness: the ground station must track both missile and target accurately and the command link adds lag and can be jammed, while the missile cannot correct on its own.

quiz.q: Why do classical guidance laws need a modern patch against a manoeuvring target?
quiz.a: Their zero-miss condition is derived assuming a non-manoeuvring target. A target that turns adds an unknown acceleration term to the engagement, so miss distance grows unless the missile has acceleration margin. Modern laws estimate or model that term, minimise a cost, or force the error to zero robustly.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry a guidance law is first flown in a hardware-in-the-loop rig, with a real seeker looking at a simulated target and real fin servos moving. Model predictive control and learned policies are now tried on the guidance computer, and the seeker output is treated as a state-estimation problem before any law runs. Search for 'proportional navigation', 'guidance law design', 'differential game guidance' and 'hardware-in-the-loop missile simulation'.
